title: Playbooks, Routine and Review: Making It a Practice
description: A playbook is a form for a hypothesis — location, map, flow, target, weakens if, decision — with flow never the trigger. The reward must be at least three times the risk, size is a separate decision, and no trade is always valid. Run the same simple day, save enough to review each decision (including the ones you skipped), and judge decisions, not outcomes.
categoryDescription: Tier 4 - Playbooks, routine and honest review

sections.title: Chapter Objective
sections.introContent:
You now have every piece: the chart, the map, flow read correctly, the tools, and the discipline for when things disagree. This last chapter turns them into a practice.

It teaches four things:

1. A playbook organises a hypothesis — it doesn't make the decision
2. Risk-to-reward and size are separate decisions, and no trade is valid
3. A simple, repeatable day — and what to save
4. Review honestly: decisions, not outcomes

sections.title: A Playbook Organises a Hypothesis
sections.introContent:
A playbook is a form with the same fields every time:

| Field | Answers |
|---|---|
| **Question** | What am I testing? |
| **Location** | Where is price in the chart structure? |
| **Map** | Which nodes matter, and what regime is it? |
| **Flow** | Does it support or challenge? |
| **Target** | The next structural level |
| **Weakens if** | The concrete things that would make me wrong |
| **Decision** | Trade, wait or pass — and at what size |

Flow sits fourth. **Flow is never the trigger.**

Two example playbooks, written as teaching templates from Skylit's charts-first and Heatseeker material:

- **Floor reversal** — price at a range low, a floor node beneath. Flow supports if bullish flow shows up at the level; it challenges if heavy put buying appears right at the floor. Target: the next ceiling. Weakens if price accepts below the floor or the floor node shrinks.
- **Ceiling rejection** — price at a range high, a ceiling node above. Flow supports if bullish flow fades or bearish flow appears; persistent call buying at the level is a conflict (Chapter 9). Target: the next floor. Weakens if price accepts above the ceiling or the ceiling node shrinks.

Both still have to pass Skylit's entry checklist before they become a trade: structure on the chart, Heatseeker confluence behind the direction, and at least 3-to-1 reward with a clean entry. (The summer bootcamp's stricter version adds a mapped liquidity sweep — all four gates, or no trade.)

questions.questionText: What is a playbook?

options.text: A list of tickers to buy
A rule that fires trades automatically
A form that organises a hypothesis

questions.questionText: Where does flow sit in a playbook?

options.text: Second, right after location — flow picks which map level matters
After location and the map — it supports or challenges

questions.questionText: A trader's playbook says: "When a $1M call sweep prints, buy." What's wrong?

options.text: $1M is too low for SPY — the trigger should be $5M
It needs a Flow Score filter too, then it's complete
Nothing — a $1M sweep is institutional, so it's a valid trigger
It makes flow the trigger and skips location, the map, the target and invalidation

questions.questionText: Price is at the floor, but heavy put buying at the ask appears right at the level. In the floor-reversal playbook, what is that?

options.text: Flow that challenges the hypothesis — a conflict to resolve

questions.questionText: A floor reversal has great chart structure and strong bullish flow, but the map shows only an air pocket below — no floor node. Is it A+?

options.text: Only if the Flow Score is high
Yes — flow makes up for the map

questions.questionText: Where does a playbook's target come from?

options.text: The next structural level on the chart and the map
The top strike of the biggest print

sections.title: Risk, Size and No Trade
sections.introContent:
**Risk-to-reward comes first.** The Skylit minimum is **3 to 1 reward to risk** (Glitch also writes it 1:3, risk to reward) — the distance to target at least three times the distance to invalidation. A great read at a bad entry is a bad trade.

**Size is its own decision.** Smaller size shrinks the dollars won or lost; it doesn't turn a bad setup good. Strong flow doesn't earn a bigger position by itself, and the Trinity rule still applies — 2 of 3 means reduced size.

**No trade is a valid outcome.** Pass when price is at a midpoint, the Trinity is totally misaligned (one diverging board still leaves 2 of 3, at reduced size), you can't write a concrete "weakens if", the risk-to-reward isn't there, or the evidence is an unresolved conflict.

questions.questionText: What is the Skylit minimum reward compared with risk?

options.text: There isn't one — it depends on the flow
Reward at least equal to the risk
Reward at least 3× the risk (often written 3:1)

questions.questionText: True or false: smaller size shrinks the dollars won or lost, but it does not change whether the setup is good.
Entry 581.40, target 590, invalidation 577. What's the risk-to-reward, and what should the trader do?

options.text: About 2 to 1 — below the minimum, so wait for a better entry or pass
It doesn't matter if the flow is strong

questions.questionText: Same setup, but price pulls back to 579. Target 590, invalidation 577. What now?

options.text: Reward 11, risk 2 — 5.5 to 1, so it qualifies

questions.questionText: Flow is huge and bullish, and the trader wants to double their normal size. What's the right thinking?

options.text: Size comes from the whole read and the risk — not from how big the flow is

questions.questionText: SPY's playbook qualifies and SPX agrees, but QQQ diverges at its ceiling. What does the Trinity rule add?

options.text: Double size to make up for it
2 of 3 aligned — reduced size, at most

sections.title: A Simple, Repeatable Day
sections.introContent:
| When (New York time) | What you do |
|---|---|
| **Before the open** | Mark levels on the chart, read the maps, write your questions |
| **During the session** | Watch flow **at your planned levels**; fill in playbooks; recheck saved hypotheses when the map reshuffles |
| **After the close** | Contract totals in the Scanner — some data is still preliminary |
| **Next morning** | Check open interest on what you saved, using the actual OI date |
| **Weekly** | Review everything — wins, losses **and skipped trades** |

The routine's job is to stop you chasing: with levels and questions, flow has something to be evidence **for**.

For every setup you act on **or skip**, save: the contract and time, snapshots of the chart, map and feed, your filters, your hypothesis and the alternatives, what you knew **at that moment**, your "weakens if", and whether you traded it or only watched.

questions.questionText: What should you do before the open?

options.text: Mark levels on the chart, read the maps, and write your questions
Watch the whole feed for big prints

questions.questionText: During the session, where should you focus on flow?

options.text: Only the biggest print of the day

questions.questionText: Which setups should you save notes on?

options.text: Both the trades you took and the ones you skipped

questions.questionText: A trader starts the session with no levels marked and trades the first big sweep. What did the routine exist to prevent?

options.text: Chasing — trading flow with no plan to test it against

questions.questionText: Why save what you knew at that moment?

options.text: So later information doesn't rewrite the decision

questions.questionText: A trader writes a setup's notes after it works out. What's the problem?

options.text: The notes are written with hindsight — they can't show what was known at the time
Notes should only be written for losers

sections.title: Review Honestly
sections.introContent:
- **Judge the decision, not the outcome.** A good decision can lose; a bad one can win. A winning trade taken at a midpoint was still a bad decision.
- **Count the misses, not just the wins.** Review only the winners and every pattern looks brilliant.
- **Keep the skipped trades.** They show whether your filter for passing is working.

The goal isn't to feel good about your trading. It's to find out what's true about it.

questions.questionText: What should a review judge?
True or false: a winning trade was always a good decision.
A trader bought calls off a mid-range sweep without checking the map, and it worked. How should the review mark it?

options.text: Good decision — the sweep was the edge and it paid
Good decision, but size should have been smaller
Neutral — outcome and process balance out
Bad decision, good outcome — a mistake, even though it made money

questions.questionText: A complete floor-reversal playbook at 5.5 to 1 stopped out on acceptance below the floor. How should the review mark it?

options.text: A reason to double size next time
Good decision, bad outcome — the "weakens if" did its job

questions.questionText: A trader reviews only their five best trades and concludes their method works. What's wrong?

options.text: They should review only the worst trades
Without the losses and skipped trades, any method looks like it works

questions.questionText: Which statement best describes "no trade"?

options.text: Something to avoid by lowering standards
A valid outcome — often the disciplined one
A failure to find a setup

sections.title: Case Study Example
sections.introContent:
*Hypothetical — constructed for teaching.*

**The playbook, filled in for SPY:** range 578–590, floor node at 578, King Node ceiling at 590, positive gamma; bull call spread flow with open interest growth — **supports**. Target 590. Weakens if price accepts below 578 — invalidation at 577.

**The decision:** at 581.40, reward to 590 is 8.60 and risk to 577 is 4.40 — about **2 to 1**, below the minimum. The trader **waits**. At 579, reward is 11 and risk is 2 — **5.5 to 1**. Now it qualifies.

**The week, reviewed:**

- **Monday** — that floor reversal at 579 hit its target. *Good decision, good outcome.*
- **Tuesday** — bought calls off a mid-range QQQ sweep without checking the map. It worked. *Bad decision, good outcome.*
- **Wednesday** — waited on an unresolved conflict at the 590 ceiling; price broke out. *Good decision, missed move.*
- **Thursday** — a complete floor reversal stopped out on acceptance below the floor. *Good decision, bad outcome.*

One mistake — and it was Tuesday's win.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.introContent:
### Mistake 1 — Treating a playbook as a trigger

A playbook is a checklist for a hypothesis. It doesn't fire trades on its own.

---

### Mistake 2 — Taking a good read at a bad entry

If the reward isn't at least three times the risk, wait or pass.

---

### Mistake 3 — Grading trades by profit

A win at a midpoint was still a bad decision; a clean stop-out on a complete playbook was a good one.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
sections.introContent:
- A playbook is a form: question, location, map, flow, target, weakens if, decision. Flow is never the trigger.
- A trade needs chart structure, Heatseeker confluence and at least 3-to-1 reward with a clean entry — the bootcamp adds a mapped sweep as a fourth gate.
- Minimum risk-to-reward is 3 to 1. Size is separate. No trade is valid.
- Run the same day; save enough to review trades **and** skips.
- Judge decisions, not outcomes — and count the misses.

***Remember:***

***A large print earns investigation. It does not identify a profitable trade.***
